strengths: Addresses a useful robotics problem: improving action selection without training or deploying an external verifier. The method can operate on existing autoregressive VLAs, with optional condition-dropout fine-tuning.

Evaluation spans three simulation benchmarks, two VLA architectures, and real Franka experiments. RoboCasa results demonstrate improvements across demonstration budgets, and the real-world OOD experiment provides encouraging evidence for the training-free variant.

Table 5 includes useful ablations of joint training, selection criteria, masking variants, reference temperature, and token aggregation. Shared-prefill deployment also meaningfully reduces the overhead of parallel sampling.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol risks selection bias. Appendix A.3 searches sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature on each dataset and reports the best result, without describing a separate validation set or held-out final evaluation. This is particularly concerning because performance is sensitive to these choices and several gains are small. Final configurations and comparable tuning budgets for baselines are also missing.

Evidence for the distinctive selection metric is limited. On RoboCasa, MG-Select improves over likelihood selection by only 0.5 percentage points on pick-and-place and 1.3 points overall (Table 5a). Joint training alone raises pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, with MG-Select adding another 2.5 points (Table 5d). Comparable controls separating training gains from selection gains are absent on LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world ID tasks. Consequently, the headline improvements do not establish a substantial advantage for masking-guided selection itself.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported despite averaging simulation results over three seeds. LIBERO average gains are only 1.1–1.6 percentage points, with regressions on Spatial and Goal suites. Real-world evaluation uses only 24 trials per ID task and 16 per OOD task, without confidence intervals or sufficient detail about matched initial conditions. These results do not establish the reliability of the claimed improvements.

The confidence interpretation is insufficiently supported. Masking conditions does not guarantee maximum uncertainty, and a large KL divergence between masked and conditioned predictions can indicate conditioning sensitivity rather than action correctness or precision. No direct relationship between the score and action quality is demonstrated. Indeed, the unsoftened masked reference underperforms uniform KL, and performance depends strongly on temperature and truncation to five tokens. Changing the ranking rule also cannot resolve identical candidates caused by concentrated sampling distributions.

Novelty and comparative positioning remain limited: the method combines existing distributional self-certainty ideas with condition masking and dropout training. Comparisons against likelihood and uniform-KL selection appear only in one RoboCasa setting, and there is no empirical comparison with the external-verifier methods used to motivate the work. The resulting accuracy–compute and generalization tradeoffs remain unclear.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The 168% relative gain corresponds to success increasing from 5.3% to 14.2% and includes joint training; success does not consistently improve across all task groups, and increasing candidate count beyond four does not improve performance. Precision is inferred mainly from task success rather than measured directly. Latency is reported per episode, without per-decision timing, deployment hardware, or enough implementation detail to substantiate practical control-rate claims.

strengths: Addresses a relevant robotics problem: improving action selection without training or deploying a separate verifier. The proposed masked-conditioning KL score is straightforward to integrate into autoregressive VLAs.
Evaluation spans three simulation benchmarks, two VLA backbones, and real-robot experiments. RoboCasa includes three demonstration budgets, and simulation results are averaged over three seeds.
Reported improvements are promising, including real-world success increases from 37.5% to 47.9% on ID tasks and 53.1% to 71.9% on OOD tasks.
The component ablations and shared-prefill implementation provide useful practical evidence, including a substantial latency reduction relative to naive parallel sampling.
weaknesses: The distinctive selection metric provides limited improvement over simpler alternatives. In Table 5(a), MG-Select exceeds likelihood selection by only 0.5 percentage points on pick-and-place and 1.3 points overall; uniform-KL selection is also close. These comparisons appear only on one benchmark and demonstration budget, without uncertainty estimates. The evidence does not establish a substantial contribution beyond existing self-certainty-based best-of-N selection.

Much of the headline improvement is attributable to joint training rather than the proposed inference criterion. In Table 5(d), joint training alone raises pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, while adding MG-Select raises it to 31.0%. Corresponding joint-training-only controls are missing for the 30-demonstration headline result, LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world ID evaluation, preventing attribution of those gains to test-time selection.

The model-selection protocol raises a significant evaluation concern. Appendix A.3 searches sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature and reports the best result for each policy, but identifies no separate validation set or held-out selection protocol. Selected configurations are also omitted. This leaves potential selection bias unresolved, particularly for small gains and OOD claims.

The confidence interpretation is insufficiently supported. Masking conditions does not guarantee maximum uncertainty, and a large KL(Q||P) measures distributional disagreement rather than action correctness. No calibration or candidate-ranking analysis connects this score to successful execution. Moreover, the score depends on token prefixes rather than directly on the sampled token; aggregating only the first five positions leaves the remaining action sequence unassessed.

Statistical support is inadequate for several conclusions. Simulation tables omit dispersion despite using three seeds, and real-world OOD evaluation contains only 16 trials per task across two tasks. LIBERO gains average just 1.1–1.6 points and include regressions on Spatial and Goal. These results warrant more restrained claims of consistent improvement and generalization.

The central comparison with verifier-based approaches is missing. Although their training costs and generalization limitations motivate the paper, there is no direct success-versus-compute comparison. Likelihood and uniform-KL baselines should also be evaluated across the principal benchmarks using matched tuning and computational budgets.

The broader precision and scaling claims exceed the evidence. Precision is inferred mainly from task success and qualitative examples, without quantitative manipulation-error measurements. Performance peaks at four candidates and declines with additional sampling, while reference temperature and token truncation materially affect results. The latency study reports episode-level inference time without sufficient detail on hardware, per-decision latency, or accounting for masked-reference computation.

These comparisons are restricted to one benchmark and demonstration setting, without uncertainty estimates or evidence of matched tuning budgets.

Joint training accounts for much of the headline improvement, complicating attribution to verifier-free sampling. On RoboCasa with 100 demonstrations, joint training alone raises pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, while adding MG-Select reaches 31.0%. Joint-training-only controls are missing for LIBERO, SIMPLER, real-world ID tasks, and the highlighted 30-demonstration result.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving autoregressive robot policies at inference time without training or deploying an external verifier. The condition-masked reference distribution is a simple, potentially useful adaptation of distributional self-certainty.
Evaluation spans RoboCasa, SIMPLER, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-robot tasks, with additional experiments on OpenVLA and MiniVLA. RoboCasa also demonstrates improvements without joint training.

The paper includes substantial component ablations, training configurations, failure examples, and an external-verifier comparison. Shared-prefill deployment provides a practical efficiency improvement; Table 14 reports similar success to the adapted RoboMonkey baseline with lower latency.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol leaves a substantial model-selection concern unresolved. Appendix A.3 searches sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature, then reports the best result for each policy, without identifying a separate validation set or held-out selection protocol. Given the extensive search and often modest improvements, independent evaluation and comparable baseline tuning are essential.

There is an important inconsistency between the score definition and the aggregation analysis. Under Section 3.2, the first-token KL depends only on the common observation, instruction, and empty action prefix, so it is identical across candidates. Consequently, 'First 1' cannot meaningfully rank candidates. Yet Table 12 reports this as the best aggregation strategy and interprets it as evidence for token-span tuning. The implementation, indexing, and tie-breaking require clarification; as written, this result instead suggests that sampling and training can explain the improvement without informative selection.

Most headline comparisons confound joint training with inference-time selection. In Table 5(d), joint training alone raises RoboCasa pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, while selection adds only 2.5 percentage points. Joint-training-only controls are absent from the principal SIMPLER, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world ID comparisons. On the jointly trained RoboCasa model, MG-Select exceeds likelihood selection by only 0.5 points on pick-and-place and 1.3 points overall.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported despite averaging simulation results over three seeds. Real-world evidence uses only 24 trials per ID task and 16 per OOD task, without confidence intervals or repeated training runs. These omissions make it difficult to assess small improvements or establish superiority over simpler selectors.

The central interpretation of KL divergence as action confidence is insufficiently validated. Large divergence from a masked policy measures sensitivity to conditioning, which need not imply correctness or precision. The entropy-temperature theorem establishes a standard softmax property, not the reliability of the ranking criterion. Candidate-level success prediction or controlled ranking analyses would provide stronger evidence than a single successful trajectory visualization.

The contribution beyond existing self-certainty selection and condition dropout is relatively incremental, and its generality is overstated. Performance depends strongly on reference temperature and token truncation; the untempered masked reference underperforms uniform KL, scaling beyond four candidates is nonmonotonic, and some LIBERO suites regress. The adapted RoboMonkey comparison is useful but removes components of that method and covers only one benchmark, limiting broader claims about verifier-based alternatives.

Evaluation is broad, covering RoboCasa, SIMPLER, LIBERO, CALVIN, three model sizes or families, and real-robot experiments. RoboCasa also demonstrates improvements without joint training.

The paper includes meaningful component ablations, implementation details, failure visualizations, and an external-verifier comparison. Shared-prefill deployment provides a practical efficiency improvement.

weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish a clean separation between hyperparameter selection and testing. Appendix A.3 searches sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature for each dataset and reports the best result, without specifying held-out validation. This creates a substantial selection-bias concern, particularly for small evaluation sets and modest gains. Final configurations and equivalent tuning budgets for baselines are also insufficiently documented.

The distinctive selection rule contributes relatively little beyond simpler alternatives in the main controlled comparison. Table 5(a) gives 31.0% versus 30.5% pick-and-place success and 48.1% versus 46.8% overall success compared with likelihood selection. Joint training alone increases pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%. Although this decomposition is provided for RoboCasa, corresponding joint-training-only and simple-selection controls are missing across most other benchmarks, limiting attribution of the headline gains.

There is an unresolved inconsistency in the scoring formulation. Under Section 3.2, the first-token KL depends on the shared observation, instruction, and empty action prefix, so it is identical across candidates. Consequently, the 'First 1' strategy in Table 12 cannot distinguish candidates using the stated score, yet it is presented as the strongest aggregation strategy there. The implementation, indexing, and tie-breaking require clarification.

The confidence interpretation is insufficiently supported. A large KL divergence between masked and conditioned predictions measures sensitivity to conditioning, not necessarily action correctness or precision. The paper provides no systematic candidate-ranking or calibration analysis against actual outcomes. Appendix E proves the standard entropy–temperature relationship, but does not validate the proposed ranking criterion. Changing the ranking rule also cannot resolve identical candidates caused by concentrated sampling distributions.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported despite averaging simulation results over three seeds. This matters for small differences such as the 1.1-point LIBERO improvement and for real-world experiments with only 16 or 24 trials per task. Several suites regress, and scaling beyond four candidates is nonmonotonic. These results support a more qualified claim than consistent precision improvement.

Novelty is incremental relative to the cited self-certainty approach: the main changes are a masked reference distribution, condition dropout, and tuned token aggregation. The RoboMonkey comparison is useful but removes parts of its original procedure and covers only SIMPLER. Together with the evaluation concerns above, the evidence does not yet establish that the specific methodological contribution is competitive for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: improving autoregressive VLA action selection without training or deploying an external verifier. The condition-masked reference distribution is a plausible adaptation of distributional self-certainty to robotics.
Evaluation is broad, covering RoboCasa, SIMPLER, LIBERO, CALVIN, three model scales, and real-world manipulation. RoboCasa also includes multiple demonstration budgets.

There is evidence of improvement without joint training: on RoboCasa with 100 demonstrations, MG-Select increases pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 22.6%. Real-world OOD success increases from 53.1% to 71.9%, albeit with limited trials.

The paper provides extensive component ablations, training configurations, failure visualizations, and a useful deployment optimization. Appendix D.4 also compares against an external verifier, obtaining similar success with lower latency.
weaknesses: A mathematical inconsistency undermines an important ablation. Under Section 3.2, the first-token score KL(Q1||P1) depends on the observation and empty action prefix, so it is identical across candidates. Consequently, 'First 1' aggregation cannot meaningfully rank candidates. Yet Appendix D.2 reports this as the best SIMPLER selection strategy. The implementation, indexing, and tie-breaking must be clarified before these results can support the proposed mechanism.

The evaluation protocol risks substantial selection bias. Appendix A.3 searches sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature for each dataset and reports the best result, without identifying a separate validation set or held-out final evaluation. The selected configurations are also not fully reported. This is especially concerning when improvements are small.

The incremental contribution of masked-reference selection is modest relative to simpler alternatives. In Table 5(a), likelihood selection achieves 30.5%/46.8% pick-and-place/all-task success versus 31.0%/48.1% for MG-Select. Joint training alone raises pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, accounting for most of the combined improvement to 31.0%. Equivalent training-only and likelihood-selection controls are missing from most benchmarks and real-world evaluations.

Statistical uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Although many simulation results average three seeds, no standard deviations or confidence intervals are provided. Real-world OOD evaluation uses only 16 trials per task, and ID evaluation uses 24. These results are encouraging but do not establish the reliability of the claimed gains, particularly against competitive selection baselines.

The central interpretation of KL divergence as action confidence or precision remains weakly supported. Large divergence can reflect sensitivity to removed conditions rather than correctness, and the score evaluates prefix-conditioned distributions rather than the sampled token directly. Appendix E proves only the standard entropy–temperature relationship; the single successful trajectory in Figure 5 does not establish that higher scores predict better candidate outcomes.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Most benchmark results use additional joint training despite the emphasis on requiring no additional training; some LIBERO suites regress; and candidate scaling is nonmonotonic. The RoboMonkey comparison removes parts of its original pipeline, supporting a controlled verifier comparison rather than superiority over the full method. Overall, the breadth and promising gains do not yet outweigh the unresolved scoring and evaluation issues.
